newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE- Hoax Diana video calls UK press freedom into question.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- Hoax Diana video calls UK press freedom into question.

text.p: Snatched holiday snaps, intimate phone calls, half-clothed princesses -- hardly a day passes without the private lives of Britain's rich and famous making very public newspaper headlines.

But the tabloid press may have gone too far when in the space of a week it ran three scandalous stories about the royal family, one of which turned out to be a hoax, one totally fictitious and the third was halted by a court order.

Unfettered by the kind of privacy laws enjoyed by France and tempted by a rich diet of scandal flowing from the royal family and an array of pop stars, Britain's press has been warned more than once that it "is drinking at the last chance saloon."

Now an embarrassing hoax video purporting to show Princess Diana frolicking with her former lover and an entirely false story about 14-year-old Prince William's first girlfriend have called into question the current system of press self-regulation.
Prime Minister John Major's wife Norma, not usually known for public pronouncements, supported calls for tougher privacy rules.
"I don't think the public has a right to know everything and be everywhere," said Norma Major, whose family was snapped by paparazzi photographers during their summer holiday in France.
"Your house and your garden, that should be sacrosanct ... or if you're doing something which is obviously private, and I think holiday obviously is private," she added.
Queen Elizabeth made a rare bid for privacy in August when she banned four freelance photographers from taking pictures on her Balmoral estate in Scotland during her annual summer break.
The same month, Princess Diana, the most photographed woman in the world, took out an injunction against a freelance photographer who she said was hounding her.
The government has so far resisted introducing a privacy law and newspaper editors oppose any curbs that would also restrict them exposing hypocrisy and crooked business practices.

"Members of parliament are always looking for an excuse to shut newspapers up and if they can find an excuse like this to bring in a privacy law they will, and that is why it is so damaging," said Alan Rusbridger, editor of the left-leaning Guardian newspaper which is currently campaigning against sleaze in parliament.

Lord Wakeham, chairman of the Press Complaints Commission (PCC) set up by the newspaper industry in 1991, fired a warning shot this month saying that the self-regulation system was in danger of being undermined.
But he said no one would benefit from statutory controls and suggested that the rich and famous sometimes had only themselves to blame for unwelcome attention.
"Those who seek the limelight of publicity should always be prepared when its glare is returned, sometimes harshly," Wakeham wrote in a letter to The Times.
Piers Morgan, editor of the tabloid Daily Mirror, which ran transcripts of frank conversations between the Duchess of York ("Fergie") and her spiritual guru, echoed the sense of double standards.

"We have to ask ourselves in the case of the royal family what damage is done to children by a Panorama (television) interview or someone going and talking about intimate details of their lives to a Greek mystic.
"I think that some self-regulation by the royal family wouldn't go amiss," Morgan said.
Victims of press excesses can complain for free to the PCC or take legal action under British libel laws -- although in practice high costs mean this is an option only for the rich.
The PCC says that only about 10 percent of complaints cover the privacy and public interest sections of the 18-point code of practice for journalists.

"Trying to define privacy and public interest are tasks which have foxed politicians for generations and are a good example of how a statutory system would be very difficult," a PCC spokesman told Reuters.
"The industry is deeply committed to making self-regulation work...They will do anything they can to avoid critical censure from us," the spokesman added.
Lord Wakeham said the newspaper industry had made "tremendous strides in the last few years in raising standards."
Most newspaper editors have the code of practice written into their contracts and accept that the grey area of privacy needs tightening up if statutory controls are to be avoided.

"I am in favour of reviewing the code and strengthening it...generally in the area of privacy. People's privacy needs to be protected and there are some loopholes now where it isn't quite clear how far one can go," said Daily Express editor Richard Addis.
Addis, whose paper had to apologise for a story about a supposed romance involving Diana's teenage son Prince William, said the apology was by far the most effective sanction against newspapers.
"We all hate doing it, it does damage to our relationship with our readers because it means they lose a certain amount of confidence in what we are saying," Addis said.
